title: Bringing it together
summary: The same hospital floor, now on Wi-Fi 7: what changes for each device, and what to plan.

opener.promise: What Wi-Fi 7 changes on the floor, in one view
opener.problem: Eight chapters of features; the decision needs one picture and a short plan.

beats.heading: The same hospital, on Wi-Fi 7

caption.headline: The same hospital, on Wi-Fi 7
caption.takeaway: Every kind of device on the floor gains something different from Wi-Fi 7.

beats.body:
Back on the floor where we started. Badges keep calls steady by using more than one band {{mlo-bands}}. Location tags and badges sleep between agreed wake-ups, so batteries last the shift {{twt-what}}. Pumps and staff devices sign in with [[wpa3|WPA3]], which Wi-Fi 7 and the 6 GHz band require {{wpa3-6ghz-required}} {{wpa3-mlo-required}}.

Workstations move large images faster on wide 6 GHz channels {{width-320-vs-160}}, crowded units serve many devices per transmission {{ofdma-ax}}, and alarms are designed to wait less behind other traffic {{be-latency-objective}}.
beats.bottomLine: Wi-Fi 7 is not one feature: each chapter fixes a different problem on the same floor.
beats.sceneDescription: The hospital floor from the first chapter, full of devices and busy with traffic flowing to the access points. A label above one of each kind of device names its gain: voice badges, steadier calls with multi-link; infusion pumps, safer sign-in with WPA3; patient monitors, alarms on time; phones, room for everyone with OFDMA; workstations, big files fast on 6 GHz; location tags, batteries that last the shift with TWT.

callout.title: What Wi-Fi 7 brings
points: Wide, clean 6 GHz channels, twice as wide as before{{width-320-vs-160}}
Longer battery life and alarms that wait less{{twt-what}}
[[wpa3|WPA3]] as the baseline, not an option{{wpa3-6ghz-required}}

questions.q: Which chapter matters most for us?
questions.a: Start with today's biggest pain point: crowded units point to density and 6 GHz, dropped calls to multi-link, battery swaps to Target Wake Time, and audit findings to WPA3.

beats.heading: What to plan

caption.headline: What to plan
caption.takeaway: Check devices, survey for 6 GHz, ready the wired side, and pilot before rollout.

beats.body:
The gains arrive as devices that support them join the network, so start with an inventory: which badges, pumps, monitors and phones support Wi-Fi 7, WPA3 and Target Wake Time.

Then survey before placing access points, because walls weaken 6 GHz signals more than the older bands {{6ghz-building-loss}}. Plan switch ports and power for the new access points alongside the wireless design, and pilot alarm, voice and imaging traffic on a busy unit before rolling out.
beats.bottomLine: Plan Wi-Fi 7 with the device refresh, the wired upgrades and a pilot on a real unit, not as an access-point swap alone.
beats.sceneDescription: The camera pulls back over the whole hospital floor on Wi-Fi 7, with traffic flowing to the access points, while the planning checklist appears beside it.

callout.title: Before you roll out
points: List which devices support Wi-Fi 7, WPA3 and [[twt|TWT]]
Survey for 6 GHz before placing access points{{6ghz-building-loss}}
Plan switch ports and power for new access points
Pilot alarms, voice and imaging on a busy unit

questions.a: No. Wi-Fi 8 (IEEE 802.11bn) is still in development{{wifi8-status}}; Wi-Fi 7 is the certified generation today, and device, survey and wired work done now carries forward.
